title: Roys Wedding

jokes.text: Pam introduces the chore wheel concept in a talking head — a non-spinning wheel she calls a wheel.
jokes.setup: Pam announces she has 'created the chore wheel' to solve the filth problem during the custodian's absence.
jokes.punchline: The wheel doesn't spin — it's just a static chart moved one notch per day, subverting the entire premise of a 'wheel.'
jokes.explanation: A solid cold-open premise joke. Pam's earnest practicality clashing with the office's desire for fun is classic character comedy. The non-spinning wheel is a small but genuine subversion of expectations.

jokes.text: "A wheel is supposed to spin." / "No, I'm familiar with spinning. It's just, that wouldn't work with a chore wheel, because people might get the same chore." / "Bah! Boring. All she talks about is chores."
jokes.setup: Kevin complains the wheel should spin; Pam explains logically why it can't.
jokes.punchline: Kevin dismisses her entire explanation with 'Bah! Boring. All she talks about is chores' — completely ignoring that a chore wheel is supposed to be about chores.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's oblivious complaint is deeply character-specific — his complete inability to engage with the actual purpose of the chore wheel is perfectly Kevin. 'All she talks about is chores' as a complaint about the chore wheel is a tight piece of absurd logic.

jokes.text: "A wheel wants to spin, Pam. Spinning would be more fun." — Dwight in talking head
jokes.setup: The debate about the wheel spinning has been established in the cold open.
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers his verdict in a solemn talking head as if this is an important philosophical position, agreeing with Kevin's frivolous complaint.
jokes.explanation: Dwight siding with Kevin on the spinning wheel against Pam's pragmatism is a funny character inversion — Dwight the efficiency expert agrees the wheel should be more fun. The deadpan delivery elevates a simple callback.

jokes.text: The office has rigged the chore wheel to actually spin — reaction shot of the office cheering as the wheel spins.
jokes.setup: Pam insisted the wheel couldn't spin or people would get the same chore.
jokes.punchline: The office ignores her and rigs it to spin anyway, with enthusiastic cheers — proving they cared more about fun than chores.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying visual payoff to the spinning wheel debate. The office's collective rebellion against Pam's sensible solution is a good ensemble moment.

jokes.text: "This sucks. Yeah, seriously. It's like everything on there is work." / "Yeah, and I don't think that you understand wheels."
jokes.setup: Kevin lands 'Mug duty' on the newly spinning chore wheel.
jokes.punchline: Kevin complains it's all work — missing that it's literally a chore wheel — then delivers the callback 'you don't understand wheels' as a retort to Pam's defense.
jokes.explanation: 'I don't think you understand wheels' as a retort to Pam explaining the literal purpose of a chore wheel is a tight piece of circular logic. Kevin weaponizing his earlier complaint as a debate-ender is good character comedy.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'I've been through several rounds of development with the team...' — revealing the chore wheel has now become a prize/penalty wheel with no chores on it.
jokes.setup: Pam presented a practical chore wheel. The office wanted it to spin and be fun.
jokes.punchline: 'The one thing that is not on the chore wheel is chores. But they were right, it's more fun this way.' Pam has completely capitulated and lost the plot.
jokes.explanation: This is a well-earned escalation payoff. The show sets up Pam's sensible chore wheel, the office rebels, and the punchline is that through 'several rounds of development' the wheel now has zero chores on it. 'But they were right, it's more fun this way' is Pam's resigned acceptance delivered with perfect Office deadpan. The structure is excellent — setup, escalation, subversion, acceptance. Approaches 8 territory for structure and payoff.

jokes.text: "Tiny Wheel! Tiny Wheel! Tiny Wheel!" — the office chanting around a tiny version of the wheel
jokes.setup: The chore wheel has devolved into a prize/penalty wheel. The office has apparently also created a tiny supplementary wheel.
jokes.punchline: A miniature version of the wheel exists and the office chants for it with the energy of a game show audience.
jokes.explanation: The tiny wheel is a perfect absurdist capper to the chore wheel saga. The chanting raises the energy unexpectedly and the visual of a tiny wheel being treated with reverence is inherently funny.

jokes.text: "The Tiny Wheel actually does have chores. It's so cute, no one seems to mind." Then someone lands on 'Toilets!' and seems unbothered.
jokes.setup: The main wheel lost all its chores through development. Pam reveals the tiny wheel has the actual chores.
jokes.punchline: 'It's so cute, no one seems to mind' — the chores were successfully disguised by making the wheel adorable. Cuteness defeated practicality concerns.
jokes.explanation: Excellent button to the cold open. The insight that 'cute = compliance' is a sharp observational joke about human psychology, and Pam delivering it with genuine satisfaction ('she's won') is great character work. The someone landing on 'Toilets!' and being fine is perfect visual confirmation. This rivals joke #6 as the best cold-open moment.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'I think the only weird thing about going to your wife's ex-fiancé's wedding on a weekday at 8:00 a.m. is that it's your wife's ex-fiancé.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are getting ready to attend Roy's wedding. The situation is inherently awkward.
jokes.punchline: Jim lists 'weekday' and '8 a.m.' as weird factors before revealing the actually weird thing — they're going to Pam's ex-fiancé's wedding — delivered with calm Jim-logic.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim misdirection — he leads with two genuinely odd details (weekday, 8 a.m.) to set up the real punchline, which is burying the enormous elephant in the room under a muted 'that's the only weird thing.' The 'Thanks, Mom!' tag suggests his mom is with them and he's cutting off her commentary, adding a nice layer. Strong character integration — this is quintessentially Jim's voice.

jokes.text: Pam: 'I'm afraid he's only going to have hot dogs.' / Jim: 'Come on. Not even Roy would have hot dogs at his wedding.' / Pam: 'I planned a wedding with him. He wanted hot dogs.'
jokes.setup: Pam accepts a banana for the road to Roy's wedding. Jim reassures her the food will be fine.
jokes.punchline: Pam reveals she has insider knowledge: Roy literally wanted hot dogs at their planned wedding.
jokes.explanation: Very economical. Three lines, perfectly structured. Roy wanting hot dogs at his wedding is specific enough to be funny and entirely consistent with the Roy we knew from earlier seasons. Pam's 'I planned a wedding with him' as the credentials for her hot-dog fear is a great callback to the show's history.

jokes.text: Jim's silent reaction to the hot dog revelation — 'It's so weird.' Beat of silence, then a look to camera.
jokes.setup: Pam confirms Roy wanted hot dogs at their would-be wedding.
jokes.punchline: Jim's quiet 'It's so weird' — not about Roy having hot dogs, but about the whole situation of going to this wedding.
jokes.explanation: A quiet transitional beat. Jim's understated 'It's so weird' lands because of the accumulated awkwardness of the situation. Not a big laugh but a consistent character moment.

jokes.text: Pete opens a letter addressed to 'Customer Service' with excitement, only to be told it's not his personal mail.
jokes.setup: Pete is told he has mail. He gets excited — 'I got something?'
jokes.punchline: Pam clarifies it's addressed to Customer Service, not Pete personally. His excitement deflates immediately.
jokes.explanation: A small, relatable cringe moment. Pete's vulnerability ('I got something?') is endearing. The joke is slight but functional — it establishes Pete as a character who craves recognition.

jokes.text: 'Oh, yeah. I accidentally read it. It's not a nice letter.' — about the already-opened Newsweek
jokes.setup: Pete is excited maybe it's a nice letter. Pam notes the letter is already open.
jokes.punchline: Pam casually admits she 'accidentally' read it — a transparent lie — and confirms it's not nice.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan 'I accidentally read it' — after clearly having opened someone else's mail — is a good small lie delivered with perfect Office nonchalance. Tight and well-constructed.

jokes.text: 'The special projects fairy has arrived.' — Nellie entering the office
jokes.setup: Nellie announces herself grandiosely.
jokes.punchline: Kevin immediately responds: 'I know you don't really exist.' — treating 'special projects fairy' as a literal supernatural claim.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's literal interpretation of 'special projects fairy' — responding as if Nellie has made a metaphysical claim — is classic Kevin and gets a solid laugh. The joke lives entirely in Kevin's earnest delivery.

jokes.text: 'I'd like to see him piss on that one.' — Nellie in talking head about Andy rejecting her charity initiative
jokes.setup: Nellie explains Andy has rejected all her special projects. This one is about charity.
jokes.punchline: 'I'd like to see him piss on that one' — an aggressively crude expression for a supposedly charitable endeavor.
jokes.explanation: Nellie's combative edge coming through in a supposed goodwill moment. Her phrasing undercuts her charitable intentions perfectly — she's doing this to beat Andy, not to help. Functional character joke.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam arriving at what appears to be Roy's very nice house, being offered mimosas and banana peels being taken away by staff
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam expected a budget Roy-style event (hot dogs, etc.)
jokes.punchline: Roy's wedding is at a beautiful, well-staffed venue — a servant takes Pam's banana peel — completely subverting the hot dog expectation
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the banana/hot dog setup from earlier. The visual detail of a servant specifically taking the banana peel is funny and specific. Works as callback comedy.

jokes.text: Roy introduces Pam as 'My ex-fiancée. Ha-ha.' to the stranger — then Jim's reaction
jokes.setup: A stranger asks Roy who Jim and Pam are at the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Roy introduces Pam as 'my ex-fiancée' with a laugh, creating maximum awkwardness for Jim and Pam.
jokes.explanation: A reliable cringe moment. Roy's breezy casual introduction of his ex-fiancée at his own wedding is awkward in a realistic way, and Jim's reaction (visible discomfort) carries the moment.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'I started a new business with my college friend, but Pam doesn't know... Actually I did tell Pam and we decided No. But then I decided Yes anyway...'
jokes.setup: Jim is caught off-guard seeing someone he apparently knows from a new business venture.
jokes.punchline: Jim starts a cover story in the talking head, catches himself mid-lie, corrects to the truth — that he went behind Pam's back — and then trails off about the consequences.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character work. Jim — who has always been the cool, competent one — is caught lying on camera and immediately corrects himself, which is somehow worse. 'So I'm thinking there's another conversation coming' said with Jim's characteristic calm about something that is genuinely a big deal is very funny and very specific to his character. The rewatch value is high because it plants a season arc.

jokes.text: Stanley picks 'American Diabetes Association' as his charity. Nellie: 'You have diabetes, Stanley.' Stanley: 'I'm sorry, is the assignment to pick a selfish charity?'
jokes.setup: Nellie asks who filled out charity forms. Stanley chose the American Diabetes Association.
jokes.punchline: When called out for the self-serving choice, Stanley reframes it as a principled stance: 'Is the assignment to pick a SELFISH charity?' His total lack of shame is the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Stanley's diabetes has been an established running gag for years, and using it here is earned. But the real craft is in his counter — instead of being embarrassed, he pivots to make Nellie's question seem unreasonable, essentially accusing her of wanting selfishness. The logic is absurd but delivered with total conviction. 'Is the assignment to pick a selfish charity?' is highly quotable and deeply Stanley. Approaches the 8+ anchor in character integration and structure.

jokes.text: 'It's a great prank. I want to work with Jimmy Carter and help build gnomes.' — about Heifers International giving goats to poor people
jokes.setup: Someone pitches Heifers International, which gives livestock (goats) to people in need.
jokes.punchline: Kevin calls it 'a great prank' and conflates Jimmy Carter's Habitat for Humanity work with building 'gnomes' instead of homes.
jokes.explanation: Two Kevin jokes in one: (1) he thinks giving a goat to poor people is a prank, and (2) he mishears/misremembers 'homes' as 'gnomes' with complete confidence. The 'gnomes' malapropism is especially good — it's specific, unexpected, and perfectly Kevin. High character integration score.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I give to a foundation that teaches homeless children nautical flag signaling. It changes lives.'
jokes.setup: Andy is establishing his charitable credentials to counter Dwight's refusal.
jokes.punchline: Andy's charity of choice is nautical flag signaling for homeless children — a hilariously useless skill delivered with total sincerity. 'It changes lives.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedy. The specificity of 'nautical flag signaling' as the chosen skill for homeless children is perfectly absurd — it's useless, elite, and totally Andy (vaguely nautical prep-school affectation). 'It changes lives' delivered with complete sincerity is the perfect button. This is the kind of joke that's character-specific, surprising, and economical. Comfortably in 8-territory.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I will not be participating, as there is no evidence that charity works.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is sharing their chosen charities
jokes.punchline: Dwight opts out with a confident pseudo-empirical stance that charity has no evidence base
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight — confidently wrong in a very specific ideological way. 'No evidence that charity works' sounds like it could be a Dwight thesis paper. Great character economy.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I'm not doing it for you. I'm doing it for the preservation of nautical flag signaling.'
jokes.setup: Nellie thanks Andy for participating in Operation Giveback.
jokes.punchline: Andy clarifies his motivation is not charity toward people but preservation of nautical flag signaling as a practice — an even more absurd position than the first joke.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback that escalates the original joke. Andy isn't even doing it for the homeless children — he's doing it for the FLAG SIGNALING ITSELF. The selflessness of charity has been completely inverted while still sounding noble in Andy's delivery. Extremely economical and well-structured.

jokes.text: Dwight chooses the Global Relief Foundation — 'which was recently discovered to be a front for the Taliban.'
jokes.setup: Dwight, forced to participate, picks a charity.
jokes.punchline: He chose an organization that is a front for the Taliban, delivered mid-sentence with a pivot.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's commitment to a Taliban front charity as his chosen cause — whether from genuine contrarianism or actual research — is perfectly in character. The structure (letting Nellie say 'Great. Thank you...' before Dwight completes the sentence) is a textbook setup/reveal. Deeply Dwight: he researched the most subversive option possible.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Great heroin, though.' — about the Taliban
jokes.setup: Everyone has established the Taliban is terrible.
jokes.punchline: Andy suddenly adds 'Great heroin, though' — an aside that comes from nowhere, delivered casually.
jokes.explanation: A dark aside that works on economy alone — three words that land unexpectedly. The character integration is weaker (it's more of a writer's joke than specifically Andy), but the sheer brevity and timing make it effective.

jokes.text: 'The nanny state is over, ladies and gentlemen! You're welcome.' — Dwight declares victory as Nellie caves
jokes.setup: Nellie says she can't have the Taliban on the charity roster, so Operation Giveback is dead.
jokes.punchline: Dwight takes a victory lap, declaring the 'nanny state is over' — as if forcing a charity initiative is government overreach.
jokes.explanation: Dwight framing a workplace charity drive as 'the nanny state' is perfectly in character — his libertarian grandiosity applied to something comically small. 'You're welcome' as a self-congratulatory button is classic Dwight.

jokes.text: 'Is it almost time to cut the pancake or what?' — at Roy's fancy wedding breakfast
jokes.setup: Roy's wedding is at a beautiful, upscale venue with mimosas and servers.
jokes.punchline: Roy asks if it's time to 'cut the pancake' — a very Roy way to refer to whatever the elegant breakfast centerpiece is.
jokes.explanation: Roy calling the wedding cake/centerpiece a 'pancake' is consistent with his working-class bluntness and the hot dog joke earlier. Mild but character-true.

jokes.text: Roy: 'Come on, if it wasn't for you, I never would have met Lara. I mean, seriously, I kind of dodged a bullet on that one. I'm just kidding. You're welcome.'
jokes.setup: Roy is being gracious to Pam and Jim for attending. He credits Pam for how he met his new wife.
jokes.punchline: Roy says he 'kind of dodged a bullet' — referring to Pam — realizes what he's said, adds 'I'm just kidding,' then immediately replaces any apology with a smug 'You're welcome.'
jokes.explanation: This is excellent cringe comedy. Roy's social unawareness is perfectly calibrated — he means to be gracious, says something awful, offers a hollow retraction, then doubles down with the most tone-deaf possible sign-off. The 'You're welcome' is the killer — it removes any possibility he feels bad. Great character work showing that Roy has grown (he's successful, warm) but is still fundamentally Roy.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Not gravel, obviously.' — when Roy asks what Jim is up to professionally
jokes.setup: Roy reveals he started a successful gravel company. He asks what Jim's doing.
jokes.punchline: Jim reflexively clarifies 'Not gravel, obviously' — as if gravel would be an option, betraying that Roy's success is getting to him.
jokes.explanation: Three words that do a lot of work. Jim is flustered — Roy's success rattles him — and his instinct is to immediately differentiate himself from gravel, which nobody asked about. The defensiveness disguised as a casual aside is very Jim-in-insecure-mode. Extremely economical.

jokes.text: Roy's friend interrupting about the $50,000 sports car — 'Hey, bro. Stop wasting time with this haircut.'
jokes.setup: Roy is catching up with Jim and Pam. His rich friend interrupts.
jokes.punchline: The friend dismisses Jim as 'this haircut' — a casual, cutting insult — while referencing Roy's $50,000 sports car, further humiliating Jim.
jokes.explanation: 'This haircut' as a dismissive nickname for someone is a decent burn, and it reinforces the episode's theme of Jim's life being compared unfavorably to Roy's. The $50,000 sports car detail twists the knife further.

jokes.text: Clark's fake news producer pitch to Erin: 'You'll just come over, put on a little lipstick, loosen up with a glass of red wine and then we'll just run through a few stories. You know, a couple of different ways in a couple of different outfits. It'd be really tasteful...'
jokes.setup: Clark claims a 'big-time local news producer' friend wants to audition Erin for on-air talent.
jokes.punchline: Clark's pitch is transparently a sleazy come-on dressed as a professional opportunity — wine, outfits, 'tasteful' — and Erin is completely oblivious.
jokes.explanation: The humor is cringe-based — Clark's pitch is transparently creepy and Erin's earnest acceptance of it creates discomfort. The joke works because Clark is actually trying to be subtle and failing completely. The discomfort is effective but the premise isn't entirely original.

jokes.text: Clark's talking head: 'No, Clark's not my friend. He is the douche that sits next to me at the office. My friends are Scott, Glen and Rob, but you don't know them.'
jokes.setup: Clark referred to Pete as his friend while pitching Erin.
jokes.punchline: Pete uses his talking head to specifically correct the record: Clark is a 'douche,' not a friend. He even names his actual friends to prove he has them.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Scott, Glen and Rob, but you don't know them' is what makes this joke work. Pete is defensive and specific — he needs the documentary crew to know he has actual friends. The 'but you don't know them' has a hint of pathetic earnestness that's very funny.

jokes.text: Erin's talking head: 'I never really thought much about being more than a receptionist, but why? Because I happened to answer a Help Wanted ad to be a receptionist? I mean, what if the ad had been for a CEO or for a brain surgeon?'
jokes.setup: Erin is reflecting on the news audition opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Erin's logic is that she could have been a CEO or brain surgeon had she simply responded to a different help-wanted ad — as if the job defines the person, not the qualifications.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever piece of Erin character comedy. Her earnest belief that her career was an accident of job-ad browsing, and that she might just as easily have become a brain surgeon, captures her guileless worldview perfectly. The logic is charmingly broken and specific to Erin. High character integration.

jokes.text: Pam's shocked reaction as Roy sits at a piano and begins to play — 'He plays the piano? No. Roy? No.'
jokes.setup: Roy announces he has a surprise for his bride. Pam and Jim watch.
jokes.punchline: Roy sits at a grand piano and begins to play. Pam's disbelief — 'No. Roy? No.' — reflects nine seasons of knowing Roy as the opposite of this.
jokes.explanation: This moment works on multiple levels simultaneously: (1) pure comedy of Roy doing something completely contrary to his established character, (2) Pam's 'No. Roy? No.' is perfectly specific — she says his name mid-sentence as if double-checking reality, (3) the emotional undercurrent that Roy became someone different, and possibly better, for his new partner. The character integration score is extremely high because this joke is inseparable from nine seasons of Roy being an oblivious, unromantic warehouse worker.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam compete to reveal surprising things about each other — Jim tries to surprise her with the 'court-side Sixers tickets' story; Pam completes it for him.
jokes.setup: Roy's romantic surprise with the piano prompts Jim and Pam to test how well they know each other.
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'surprise' story about court-side Sixers tickets is immediately completed by Pam, including the detail that they were away games in Phoenix — deflating any mystery.
jokes.explanation: A relatable couple's joke elevated by the context of Roy's romantic surprise making them self-conscious. The 'away game in Phoenix' detail Pam adds is funny and specific, and the whole exchange carries the emotional weight of the episode's theme (do Jim and Pam still surprise each other?).

jokes.text: 'I mean, every game is an away game for one of the teams.' — Jim's philosophical defense of the Phoenix Sixers situation
jokes.setup: The tickets were useless because they were away-game tickets in Phoenix.
jokes.punchline: Jim notes philosophically that every game is an away game for one of the teams — technically true, completely irrelevant to his defense.
jokes.explanation: Jim's fake-philosophical out — a technically true but completely useless observation — is a good bit. It shows him grasping for logic while Pam (and the audience) sees through it immediately. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jim tries to tell a surprising story about his brothers tricking him with lottery numbers on tape, but Pam already knows the ending.
jokes.setup: Jim says he has a story Pam doesn't know — 'there's a funny ending I can't remember.'
jokes.punchline: Pam completes the punchline before Jim can — 'that you thought you were millionaires' — and Jim confirms it while still acting surprised at himself for forgetting his own punchline.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of the 'do we know everything about each other' theme. Pam finishing Jim's own story — including the punchline he 'can't remember' — is a sweet and funny bit. The 'Shoot! I knew that one' from Jim is a nice button.

jokes.text: Angela's talking head about 'the Senator and I still have mystery' — cut to her looking uncomfortable/uncertain at Roy's wedding
jokes.setup: Everyone is discussing whether couples still surprise each other. Angela says she and the Senator still have mystery.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm always waiting to see what he's going to surprise me with next.' — delivered with a tight smile that suggests the 'mystery' is something she suspects and fears (the Senator's closeted status).
jokes.explanation: This joke operates entirely on dramatic irony. The audience knows (or suspects) the Senator is gay; Angela claims they have 'mystery' with a forced smile. 'I'm always waiting to see what he's going to surprise me with next' is unintentionally foreboding. Extremely high character integration because the joke only works with Angela's specific storyline.

jokes.text: Dwight offers to live under Taliban law to trap Nellie into abandoning Operation Giveback.
jokes.setup: Dwight tells Nellie that since she supports the Taliban (charity), she should live by their rules.
jokes.punchline: Nellie, not catching the trap, agrees — 'Absolutely, I will.' The logic is insane but played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's logical trap — 'you support them, you should live by their rules' — is absurd but internally consistent with his character. The joke that Nellie blithely agrees reveals her own obliviousness.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'I feared Nellie had some sort of a plan. But she used a ridiculous font. You don't have a plan. When you use a ridiculous font, no one thinks you have a plan.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is analyzing Nellie's Operation Giveback strategy.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's entire counter-intelligence analysis reduces to: she used a bad font, therefore no plan. This is both a valid point and a completely reductive one.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Dwight talking head. The font-as-threat-assessment is a very specific piece of Dwight logic that is (a) absurd, (b) weirdly true, (c) delivered as tactical analysis. 'When you use a ridiculous font, no one thinks you have a plan' is highly quotable and functions as actual advice. Strong structure and economy.

jokes.text: Dwight steals Nellie's pen and taunts her: 'Oh, this is a lovely pen. And it's mine now because I stole it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to trigger Taliban law in the office so Nellie faces a punishment.
jokes.punchline: Dwight commits a theft openly and announces it with gleeful specificity: 'And it's mine now because I stole it.'
jokes.explanation: Dwight announcing his theft with legal clarity ('it's mine now because I stole it') is funny in its transparency. He's executing an absurd plan with total commitment and precision.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'That means you're not serious or someone's getting their hand cut off.'
jokes.setup: Nellie calls Dwight insane after he invokes Taliban theft punishment (hand cutting).
jokes.punchline: Dwight presents it as a binary: either she's not serious about her commitment to Taliban law, or someone's getting their hand cut off. He offers no third option.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's dark binary logic — perfectly delivered — is frightening and funny simultaneously. His commitment to the bit has escalated to genuine threat level.

jokes.text: Dwight extends his hand to be chopped off with the cleaver.
jokes.setup: Dwight has trapped Nellie into Taliban law. The logical consequence is a hand-chopping.
jokes.punchline: Dwight EXTENDS HIS OWN HAND to be chopped off — offering himself as the hand-cut victim to force Nellie into actually performing the deed or backing down.
jokes.explanation: The peak of the Dwight/Taliban escalation arc. Dwight offering his OWN hand to be chopped off is a perfect Dwight move: he has calculated that Nellie will capitulate, and he is willing to sacrifice a hand to win an office dispute. This is one of the episode's best moments — it reveals character (Dwight's fanatical commitment), escalates perfectly, and is genuinely unexpected. The absurdity of getting here through a workplace charity drive is the backbone of the joke.

jokes.text: Dwight's exit advice: 'Tie a shoe. Toss a salad. Do any of the two-hand activities that you'll miss the most.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has offered his hand and the cleaver. He gives Nellie time to prepare.
jokes.punchline: Dwight solemnly advises himself to say farewell to two-handed activities before she chops — 'Tie a shoe. Toss a salad.' delivered with the gravity of a condemned man.
jokes.explanation: A masterful button to the escalation. 'Tie a shoe. Toss a salad.' — two specific, mundane two-handed activities — delivered with complete sincerity as final farewells is deeply funny. The bathos of 'toss a salad' as something you'd miss most is perfect. The specificity elevates what could have been a generic 'things you do with two hands' joke into something quotable. Approaches the 8-anchor level.

jokes.text: Andy asks about Clark's fake news audition wardrobe for Erin — Clark specifies: button-downs, camisole, blazer, pencil skirt, stilettos ('definitely open-toed'), something low-cut ('industry secret: camera makes everything seem higher-cut'), seamed pantyhose, and a robe 'he probably has at his place.'
jokes.setup: Andy genuinely asks what Erin needs to wear for a news audition.
jokes.punchline: Clark's list escalates from professional (blazer) to increasingly inappropriate (open-toed stilettos, low-cut, seamed stockings, robe at his apartment) while Andy nods along approvingly.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Clark's wardrobe requirements is a sustained cringe joke. 'The camera makes everything seem higher-cut' as an 'industry secret' is particularly good — it sounds plausible enough for Andy to accept. The robe at his place is the closer.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'I absolutely will do that.' — then Darryl's talking head: 'Guess I'll just head over to the mall, then. Buy Erin some sexy fun outfits. That Clark, huh?'
jokes.setup: Andy gives Darryl a credit card and tells him to take Erin to the mall to get Clark's list of outfits.
jokes.punchline: Darryl accepts with enthusiasm, then in talking head reflects with barely-concealed amusement that he's being paid to take a pretty woman shopping for 'sexy fun outfits.' His shrug: 'That Clark, huh?'
jokes.explanation: Darryl's understated 'That Clark, huh?' — simultaneously acknowledging the scam and his own benefiting from it — is a perfectly calibrated reaction beat. He's the only one in the room who fully sees what Clark is doing and he's... fine with going to the mall.

jokes.text: Angela's 'oldy-weds' game comment and Kevin asking 'What's the craziest place you ever made whoopee?'
jokes.setup: The wedding party is playing a newlywed-style game. Angela calls them 'oldy-weds.'
jokes.punchline: Kevin immediately jumps to 'What's the craziest place you ever made whoopee?' as the most interesting question, which Angela shuts down.
jokes.explanation: A standard Kevin joke — inappropriate question delivered without self-awareness. 'Whoopee' is a funny word choice but the joke is fairly predictable. Angela's 'Language!' is a nice character beat but doesn't elevate it much.

jokes.text: Jim correctly guesses Pam's celebrity crush was John Stamos — then Pam reveals John Stamos was 'temporary' before Johnny Depp, then George Clooney — and Jim says 'Johnny Depp. Totally.'
jokes.setup: The game asks who Pam's first celebrity crush was. Jim answers 'John Stamos.'
jokes.punchline: Pam corrects: Stamos was temporary. She moved on quickly to Depp. Jim, pretending he knew, says 'Johnny Depp. Totally' — he clearly didn't know.
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'Johnny Depp. Totally' as damage control — pretending he knew all along — is a nice small bit. It shows Jim covering a gap in his knowledge of Pam, which feeds the episode's theme.

jokes.text: Jim apologizes: 'Sorry, I was having a separate conversation with Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Jim gives 'George Clooney' as his next answer — apparently a completely different question.
jokes.punchline: Jim clarifies he's been answering questions in a parallel conversation with Kevin, not the wedding game. The non-sequitur 'George Clooney' was for Kevin's separate question.
jokes.explanation: A small comedy of errors — Jim juggling two conversations and mixing up the answers. The 'separate conversation with Kevin' line is delivered with perfect Office-style non-explanation.

jokes.text: Jim's reaction to seeing his business partner at Roy's wedding — his talking head acknowledging 'I think maybe there actually is something I don't know about Jim.'
jokes.setup: The episode has built around the question of whether Jim and Pam still surprise each other.
jokes.punchline: Pam's talking head: 'I think maybe there actually is something I don't know about Jim.' — said with a tone that's equal parts amused and unsettled.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire Jim/Pam storyline in this episode. Pam's realization — played lightly but landing heavy — closes the loop on the 'do we still surprise each other?' arc. It's funny because of what we know (Jim went behind her back) and resonant because of what it means for their relationship. High character integration and strong earned payoff.

jokes.text: Darryl talking head: 'Andy made me his consigliere, which means assistant regional manager. I guess he thought I would be into The Godfather because I'm black. Wrong. I'm into The Godfather because I'm a cinephile. I like Scarface because I'm black.'
jokes.setup: Darryl explains his new role at the company — Andy calls him his 'consigliere.'
jokes.punchline: Darryl dismantles Andy's presumed racial logic by clarifying his appreciation for The Godfather is cinephilic, then undercuts himself by confirming he DOES like Scarface for race-based reasons — the exact thing he just denied.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The structure is perfect in three beats: (1) Andy is racially presumptuous, (2) Darryl denies it with a sophisticated alternative ('I'm a cinephile'), (3) Darryl immediately confirms the exact same logic for Scarface. The reversal is shocking because it happens so fast and Darryl's delivery is completely straight-faced. 'I like Scarface because I'm black' is a perfect punchline — it doesn't shy away from the joke, it commits to it completely. Highly quotable, specific to Darryl's character, and the structure is nearly flawless. This is the episode's anchor 8.5+ moment.

jokes.text: Andy to the office: 'I want her to feel very comfortable in her very sexy skin. So, everybody say something that you like about her body.'
jokes.setup: Andy calls a voluntary meeting to discuss Erin's confidence for the news audition.
jokes.punchline: Andy's idea of confidence-building for a news audition is asking coworkers to compliment Erin's physical attributes — completely missing the point while thinking he's helping.
jokes.explanation: Andy's well-meaning cluelessness is solid character comedy. His conflation of 'news anchor confidence' with 'people complimenting your body' is a believable Andy-ism — he's not malicious, just completely obtuse.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'I like Erin's hair. It's a very pretty color.' — as his body compliment contribution
jokes.setup: Andy asks everyone to say something nice about Erin's body.
jokes.punchline: Darryl, clearly recognizing the inappropriateness of the exercise, offers the most neutral possible 'body' compliment: her hair color.
jokes.explanation: Darryl's calculated minimal compliance is perfectly in character. He's the smartest person in the room, participating just enough to not make a scene while keeping his dignity intact.

jokes.text: Oscar calls out the absurdity of the body-compliment exercise. Andy responds: 'Newsflash, everyone, the human race finds attractive people more trustworthy.' Then: 'Walter Cronkite. Cronkite was hot! If I could go back in time, I'd take that moustache ride.'
jokes.setup: Oscar asks why they're talking about Erin's looks for a news audition instead of credibility.
jokes.punchline: Andy invokes Walter Cronkite as proof that attractive people are trusted — then declares Cronkite was 'hot' and says he'd 'take that moustache ride.'
jokes.explanation: 'I'd take that moustache ride' is the kind of absurd specific phrasing that becomes instantly quotable. Andy defending his logic by claiming Cronkite was sexually attractive — while using him as a trustworthiness example — is wonderfully chaotic. The joke escalates quickly from bad logic to completely unhinged declaration.

jokes.text: Erin's news story: 'Afghan President Hamid Karzai declared a new policy of Dollar Days throughout the country, promising low, low prices on all 2012 Kia Sentras and Sonatas. Aren't you glad you waited? Karzai commented.'
jokes.setup: Erin is doing a news audition. She has prepared a current events story.
jokes.punchline: Erin has written a story that is literally a car dealership ad transposed onto Afghan geopolitics — complete with 'Aren't you glad you waited?' as a Karzai quote.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Erin's 'news story' is a perfect synthesis of her worldview — she processed current events through the lens of local car dealership ads, the most familiar form of TV content to her. The specificity of Kia Sentras and Sonatas (not a generic car) and 'Aren't you glad you waited?' as a Karzai quote is brilliant. It's entirely character-consistent, surprising, and deeply original. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Erin: 'A little bit here, a little bit there.' — when asked where she got the story
jokes.setup: Andy asks where Erin got her Karzai/Kia story.
jokes.punchline: Erin's vague 'a little bit here, a little bit there' — as if she has sources — while the story is clearly assembled from TV ads, delivered with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: A small button to the Karzai joke. Erin's journalistic confidence about sources she definitely doesn't have is a minor but effective character beat.

jokes.text: 'I bet you didn't think I knew current events.' — Erin to Andy after the Karzai story
jokes.setup: Erin has just read a Kia car ad dressed as Afghan political news.
jokes.punchline: Erin is proud and slightly smug that she 'knows current events' — completely unaware that her story is not current events.
jokes.explanation: Erin's pride in her current events knowledge after delivering a car dealership ad as political news is perfectly consistent. Her complete lack of self-awareness is played sincerely, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Erin struggles to pause long enough after 'For Channel Eleven News' — multiple takes get increasingly desperate
jokes.setup: Andy/Clark coaches Erin to pause after 'For Channel Eleven News' before saying her name, for dramatic effect.
jokes.punchline: Erin cannot modulate the pause — she either rushes through or pauses too awkwardly — the montage of failed takes escalates the cringe.
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe sequence. Erin's inability to control the pause — turning a simple broadcast technique into an ordeal — is relatable and funny. The visual performance comedy elevates it beyond what the transcript conveys.

jokes.text: Pam invents a story about a divorced high school guy hitting on her at the mall — 'And I didn't tell you because I felt embarrassed, and I didn't know if you'd be mad, or worried.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are still trying to find things they haven't told each other. Pam offers to go first.
jokes.punchline: Pam constructs a fake oversharing confession — then Jim immediately calls it: 'That didn't happen. You would have told me right away.'
jokes.explanation: Pam trying to manufacture a secret — and Jim instantly seeing through it — is a sweet character moment. Jim's 'You would have told me right away' reveals he knows her better than she knows him (because he IS hiding something). The irony is well-earned.

jokes.text: 'God, give it up, Beesly. You know me too well.' — Jim in the car after the secret game, long pause
jokes.setup: Pam is pressing Jim to reveal something she doesn't know about him.
jokes.punchline: Jim says 'God, give it up, Beesly. You know me too well.' — then there's a conspicuous silence. The joke is that he's deflecting with flattery while actually hiding something significant.
jokes.explanation: The line works because it's a classic Jim deflection — charming, intimate, seemingly genuine — that the audience knows is covering a real secret. The awkward silence that follows (implied by the timestamp gap to 18:45) is the actual punchline. Dramatic irony makes this funnier on rewatch.

jokes.text: Andy, realizing Erin's audition needs a co-anchor, suggests Pete because 'he's already got rapport with Erin' — then Andy inserts himself as co-anchor instead.
jokes.setup: Andy tells Erin the audition needs to show how she relates to a news team. Clark can't co-anchor because he's on camera.
jokes.punchline: Andy builds to suggesting 'somebody who's already got rapport with Erin' — setting up Pete — then appears on set himself as co-anchor.
jokes.explanation: Andy's maneuver to insert himself into Erin's audition — nominally to help, actually for himself — is consistent with his Season 9 characterization. The setup/reveal structure works though it's not particularly surprising.

jokes.text: Dwight brings '127 Hours' as 'inspiration' for Nellie's hand-chopping decision — 'No, no, no! No spoilers, please.'
jokes.setup: The hand-chopping standoff is ongoing. Dwight arrives with a movie.
jokes.punchline: Dwight brings '127 Hours' — the film about a man who cuts off his own arm — as 'inspiration.' When someone objects, Dwight apologizes for spoilers, as if the movie is just a movie and not a pointed threat.
jokes.explanation: Bringing '127 Hours' as 'inspiration' for the hand-chopping standoff is inspired dark comedy. The joke works on two levels: (1) the specific film choice is perfect, (2) Dwight's 'No spoilers, please' treats it as a casual movie recommendation rather than psychological warfare. The plausible deniability of 'I just thought you'd like the film' while being absolutely menacing is peak Dwight. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Pete arrives as makeup guy: 'Sorry, man. Andy thought Erin needed a co-anchor. I'm his makeup guy. My hands are tied.'
jokes.setup: Clark set up the fake audition. Andy has inserted himself as co-anchor.
jokes.punchline: Pete appears as Andy's makeup guy — clearly also being used/bossed around — deadpanning 'My hands are tied' with the resignation of someone who knows exactly what's happening.
jokes.explanation: A functional small joke. Pete's resigned participation in Andy's self-promotion scheme is a decent bit, but it doesn't land particularly hard.

jokes.text: Andy's news co-anchor pun: 'You know what they say, Erin, if you can't take the heat, get out of the kitchen.' / Erin: 'Well, he tried to, but the fire door was blocked.'
jokes.setup: The news story is about a kitchen fire victim. Andy uses a news anchor platitude as a segue.
jokes.punchline: Erin takes the idiom literally — the guy in the fire story literally couldn't get out of the kitchen because the fire door was blocked — treating a cliché as if it's specific reporting.
jokes.explanation: A great Erin joke. Erin interprets Andy's clichéd news-anchor turn-of-phrase as a literal continuation of the story — creating a perfect accidental callback that is both character-true and genuinely clever. The punchline works because Erin is completely earnest, not trying to be clever. High character integration.

jokes.text: Clark immediately calls 'That's a wrap, everybody' after the first usable take — clearly trying to end things before Andy ruins the footage further.
jokes.setup: The first decent take of the fake news audition is complete.
jokes.punchline: Clark rushes to shut it down before Andy insists on more takes — 'Yup, she's done' — revealing Clark's only concern is getting rid of everyone.
jokes.explanation: Clark's urgency to shut down the shoot and dismiss people — especially Andy — is a functional character joke revealing his actual motive (the audition was a ruse). Not a big laugh but clear and economical.

jokes.text: Andy pushes for more takes: 'We could do it in a close-up. That might even be better for editing.' — clearly wanting to stay on camera
jokes.setup: Clark declares the shoot wrapped. Andy resists.
jokes.punchline: Andy's reasoning for more takes — 'better for editing' — is transparently about his own desire to be on camera, not about helping Erin.
jokes.explanation: A mild character joke about Andy's narcissism dressed as helpfulness. Functional but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Erin's talking head: 'Hey, even if this doesn't work out for me, I'm just glad I had the guts to do it. And maybe it will work out for Andy.'
jokes.setup: The fake audition is over. Erin reflects on the experience.
jokes.punchline: Erin, with complete sincerity, pivots from her own ambitions to wishing Andy success — not realizing she's been used as a vehicle for Andy's vanity project.
jokes.explanation: Erin's selfless pivot to hoping Andy succeeds — without realizing the audition was always for Andy — is a perfect character button. Her obliviousness is used to reveal something true about both characters: Erin is genuinely kind and Andy is genuinely self-serving. The joke and the pathos coexist perfectly.

jokes.text: Erin's talking head: 'Hey, even if this doesn't work out for me, I'm just glad I had the guts to do it. And maybe it will work out for Andy.'
jokes.setup: Erin reflects on the audition experience
jokes.punchline: She magnanimously pivots to hoping 'it works out for Andy' — completely unaware that the whole thing was a scam targeting her, and that Andy's interest was self-serving
jokes.explanation: The irony is rich — Erin, who was being deceived, wishes good fortune for her deceiver. Her genuineness makes it both funny and a little sad. Efficient dramatic irony delivered with Erin's characteristic warmth.

jokes.text: Dwight and Nellie watching 127 Hours: 'The way he just cuts off his arm.' / 'If you like James Franco, we really should watch Rise of the Planet of the Apes.'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Nellie are watching the arm-amputation film Dwight brought as a 'Taliban law' threat
jokes.punchline: They're now watching together like normal colleagues enjoying a movie — and Nellie recommends a James Franco double feature, completely defusing the earlier standoff
jokes.explanation: A gentle, character-based resolution to the subplot. The comedy is in how quickly the adversarial dynamic has been replaced by film criticism. Functional but not a big laugh.

jokes.text: James Franco is a genius debate: 'Well, it doesn't make you stupid.' / 'Well, yeah, it does actually. It makes you real stupid.' / 'Stupid like you. No, like you! Like you! You're the stupid one...' (ongoing)
jokes.setup: Someone notes James Franco was enrolled in graduate programs at Yale, Columbia, and NYU simultaneously.
jokes.punchline: Kevin says this doesn't make you a genius. Dwight says it doesn't make you stupid. Kevin disagrees — it makes you 'real stupid.' This devolves into 'No, like YOU' at escalating speed.
jokes.explanation: A good closing bit. Kevin's position that attending multiple elite graduate programs simultaneously 'makes you real stupid' is characteristically Kevin — he's deeply committed to a wrong opinion. The childish 'No, like YOU' devolution is a funny button for the episode, functioning like a credits roll joke.

tmdb_overview: A toast at Roy's wedding leads to Pam and Jim searching their relationships for buried secrets; Dwight reacts to Nellie's mandatory charity initiative.
